newsitem.title: GERMANY: River Oder retreats leaving trail of destruction.
newsitem.headline: River Oder retreats leaving trail of destruction.

text.p: The swollen River Oder on Germany's eastern border retreated on Wednesday, leaving behind a vast trail of mud, dead fish and waterlogged homes.

Three weeks of flooding, the region's worst in living memory, has turned a large tract of once-fertile agricultural land in the Ziltendorf basin south of Frankfurt an der Oder into a vast mosquito-infested swamp.

The stench of stagnant water hangs over the area. An eery silence pervades the villages of Aurith, Wiesenau and Brieskow-Finkenheerd still largely submerged to the rooftops after a dike broke last month and residents were evacuated.

"Our streets and squares are filled with mud and dead fish," said Ute Petzel, the mayor of Ratzdorf, further south at the confluence of the Oder and Neisse rivers where water levels were falling rapidly.
"It will be weeks before we have cleaned up the mess," she said in Ratzdorf, where relief workers were removing sandbags from the streets and pumping out water from residents' cellars.

Many evacuees are desperate to return to salvage what they can of their homes. But even now the water is retreating, German officials have warned residents not return too soon to these ghost-towns on the Oder.

"Water levels are falling fast, but this is no reason to tell people it's completely safe to return to their homes. The water pressure is so great the dike could still break," a flood crisis centre spokeswoman in the region said.
"It's calmer now. Now there is hope, but there is no euphoria because we can't say we've won the battle yet," she said.
Health officials have warned residents they could be at risk from typhoid, hepatits A and bacterial diarrhoea if they come in contact with infected water during the clean up.

Authorities launched a mass innoculations programme last week as a precaution, fearing rotting carcasses left by the floods could carry disease to waterlogged towns. Thousands of residents have so far taken part, officials say.

South of the Frankfurt an der Oder, an area of 45 cubic km was flooded. But north of the city, in the Oderbruch region, authorities let ground water increase over the last month rather than pump it into the swelling river.

"There is damage caused by ground water in the Oderbruch, by removing heavy equipment from the flood area and to farmland but it's impossible to assess the extent of this," Brandenburg state environment ministry spokesman Dieter Shuette.
The ministry has formed a working group to assess the extent of damage to farms, Schuette said, but would not have any results for a while.

In Oderbruch, around Hohenwutzen, a critical section of flood barriers holding back the river were still under immense pressure because the river was retreating very slowly, a flood crisis centre spokesman said.
Local officials said soldiers and relief workers were continuing to monitor and secure dikes all along the river but that no new tears had been found overnight.
The Oder was swollen by the same rains that caused flooding in the Czech Republic and Poland last month claiming more than 100 lives and causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl pledged up to 500 million marks ($268.3 million) in federal government aid to the region along the Oder River, calling floods there in the past weeks the "worst natural disaster ever faced by newly-unified Germany".

German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe, who was due to visit the crisis area along Germany's eastern border later in the day, has said some 10,000 troops involved in securing the dikes would stay on to join clean-up efforts.
Local officials have welcomed government proposals to create jobs for 10,000 unemployed east Germans to help with reconstruction of their devastated region.
